obviousness.e: English obvious Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English obviousness From obvious + -ness.

d.g: To do as ordered by (a person, institution etc), to act according to the bidding of.
d.x: obey the rules

d.g: To do as one is told.
d.x: Soldiers are trained to obey.

obey.e: From Middle English obeyen, from Anglo-Norman obeir, obeier et al., Old French obeir, from Latin oboediō (also obēdiō (“to listen to, harken, usually in extended sense, obey, be subject to, serve”)), from ob- (“before, near”) + audiō (“to hear”). Compare audient. …

d.g: To make dark; to overshadow.
To deliberately make more confusing in order to conceal the truth.
d.x: obfuscate facts

d.g: To alter code while preserving its behavior but concealing its structure and intent.
d.x: We need to obfuscate these classes before we ship the final release.

obfuscate.e: The adjective is first attested in 1487, in Middle English, the verb in 1536; either borrowed from Middle French obfusquer, offusquer, from Old French offusquer, or directly from Late Latin obfuscātus, offuscātus, the perfect passive participle of obfuscō, offuscō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-for …

d.g: To make (something, such as an abstract idea) possible to be perceived by the senses.
d.x: It was the unknown, objectified at last, in concrete flesh and blood, bending over him and reaching down to seize hold of him.

d.g: To treat (something) as objectively real.
d.x: The mystic objectifies a rich feeling in the pit of the stomach into a cosmology.

d.g: To treat (someone) as a mere (usually sexual) object; to sexually dehumanize (someone).
d.x: Near-synonyms: demean, fetishize

objectify.e: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁óp(i) Proto-Italic *op Latin ob Latin ob- Proto-Indo-European *(H)yeh₁- Proto-Indo-European *(H)ih₁kyeti Proto-Italic *jīkjō Proto-Italic *jakjōder. Latin iaciō Latin obiciō Latin obiectus Medieval Latin obiectum Old French objectbor. …

d.g: To rebuke or scold strongly.
To remonstrate, complain, to rail against.

objurgate.e: Borrowed from Latin obiūrgātus, perfect passive participle of obiūrgō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ob- (“to, against”) + iūrgō (“to dispute, chide”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti.

d.g: To constrain someone by force or by social, moral or legal means.
d.x: Your carelessness obliges firmness on my part.

d.g: To do (someone) a service or favour (hence, originally, creating an obligation).
d.x: He obliged me by not parking his car in the drive.

d.g: To cause somebody to feel indebted.
d.x: I am much obliged to you for your recent help.

oblige.e: From Middle English obligen, from Old French obligier, obliger, from Latin obligō, obligāre, from ob- + ligō. Doublet of obligate, taken straight from Latin.

d.g: To make cloudy.

obnubilate.e: Borrowed from Latin obnūbilātus, perfect passive participle of obnūbilō (“to cover with clouds or fog”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ob- + nūbilō (“be cloudy”), from nūbēs (“cloud”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)newdʰ- (“to cover”). …

d.g: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.
d.x: From this vantage point we can observe the behavior of the animals in their natural habitat.

d.g: To follow or obey the custom, practice, or rules (especially of a religion).
d.x: Please observe all posted speed limits.

d.g: To take note of and celebrate (a holiday or similar occurrence), to keep; to follow (a type of time or calendar reckoning).
d.x: Ye shall observe the feast of unleavened bread.

d.g: To comment on something; to make an observation.
d.x: The senator observed that the bill would be detrimental to his constituents.

observe.e: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (sarwa, “weapons, armour”), Old English searu (“device”).

d.g: To be preoccupied with a single topic or emotion.
d.x: Some people are obsessed with sports.

d.g: To dominate the thoughts of someone.
d.x: Thoughts of her obsess my every waking moment.

d.g: To think or talk obsessively about.
d.x: Stop obsessing over it, will you!

obsess.e: From Latin obsessus, perfect passive participle of obsideō (“sit on or in, remain, besiege”), from ob- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”); see sit, session, etc.; compare assess, possess.

d.g: To become obsolete.

obsolesce.e: From Latin obsolescere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”), from obs- + olesco (“to grow”). Compare adolescent.

d.g: To induce severe constipation through an intestinal blockage
To become or cause to become blocked up.
d.x: Noisy, stuffy men smelling of tobacco smoke, their minds obstipated by clogged presumptions !

obstipate.e: Borrowed from Late Latin obstipātus, perfect passive participle of obstipō (“to block, stop up”), from ob- + stipō; see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To block or fill (a passage) with obstacles or an obstacle.
To impede, retard, or interfere with; hinder.
d.x: They obstructed my progress.

d.g: To get in the way of so as to hide from sight.

obstruct.e: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).

d.g: To get hold of; to gain possession of, to procure; to acquire, in any way.
d.x: obtain permission

d.g: To exist or be the case; to hold true, be in force.
d.x: But the hostage situation no longer obtains, and so Uncle Enzo feels it important to stop Rife now, […]

obtain.e: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- + tenēre (“to hold”).

d.g: To proffer (something) by force; to impose (something) on someone or into some area.
d.x: By which we may see, that they who are not called to Counsell, can have no good Counsell in such cases to obtrude.

d.g: To become apparent in an unwelcome way, to be forcibly imposed; to jut in, to intrude (on or into).
d.x: How you can bear such recollections, is astonishing to me!—They will sometimes obtrude—but how you can court them!

d.g: To impose (oneself) on others; to cut in.
d.x: She obtruded herself upon the Queen; she protested her party views; she asked for petty favours, and attributed the refusals to the influence of Abigail.

obtrude.e: From Latin obtrūdō (“thrust off or against”), from ob- (“ob-”) + trūdō (“thrust”).

d.g: To reduce the edge or effects of; to mitigate; to dull.
d.x: Small doses of opioids are also useful in obtunding airway reflexes […]

obtund.e: Latin obtundere (“to dull", "deaden", "deafen”), from ob- (see ob-) + tundere. More at obtuse.

d.g: To block up or obstruct.
To stop up (a gun breech) so as to prevent the escape of gas when firing.

obturate.e: Borrowed from Latin obtūrātus, perfect passive participle of obtūrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

d.g: To anticipate and prevent or bypass (something which would otherwise have been necessary or required); to render (something) unnecessary.
To avoid (a future problem or difficult situation).
d.x: A mild dose of a warm active aperient to obviate costiveness, or to produce two motions daily, is generally very beneficial.

d.g: Synonym of obviative.
Synonym of obviative.
d.x: This use of the obviate deictic category—that, there, those—contrasts sharply with the use of the proximate in the body of the narrative— this, here, these.

obviate.e: First attested in 1567; borrowed from Latin obviātus, perfect passive participle of obviō (“to block, to hinder”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
